wording: Start with a reconciled trial balance and a separate tax-adjustment schedule. Operating expenditure incurred to earn, secure and maintain income is addressed by Tax Act §31. Tax depreciation is governed separately, so an accounting depreciation charge is not its own tax deduction. Business loan interest, specified financing fees and negative interest fall under §33(1)(1). Interest deducted when due but still unpaid at the end of the following income year is brought back into the original due-year income, subject to the provision's bank-credit payment test. Check related-party restrictions under §37b before allowing it. Assets acquired for resale or within the taxpayer's trading business require Tax Act §27 treatment; property held for less than two years carries a rebuttable resale-profit presumption. Ordinary unrealised asset changes are excluded under §29(2), subject to its exceptions. [Tax Act][tax]

section: ### Mixed use, change of use and ships
wording: For equipment used both privately and for business, keep an individual schedule under §7. Compute annual depreciation at an elected whole percentage up to 30% of acquisition cost in year one and unrelieved balance thereafter, subject to the DKK 150,000 acquisition-cost cap. Only the current-year business-use share of that computed depreciation is deductible. Keep both total computed depreciation and actually deducted business depreciation: disposal recapture/loss allocation under §8 uses the ratio of those cumulative amounts, with the statutory excluded-cost restriction. No depreciation is computed in the sale year. Improvements to an asset originally acquired above the cap are also excluded. [Depreciation Act §§7–10][depreciation]

wording:
1. Use pre-group ordinary losses against that company's own ordinary surplus (§6(3)). Remaining pre-group losses then shelter its own capital income, after older capital losses (§6(4)); preserve any remainder for that company's later years (§6(5)).
2. Use its own earlier group-period ordinary losses against its own ordinary surplus (§6(6)). Its remaining current/group-period ordinary losses then shelter its own current capital income, after older capital losses and pre-group ordinary losses (§6(7)).
3. Only then allocate the remaining current/group-period ordinary loss, up to the remaining combined ordinary surpluses, proportionally among the surplus companies (§6(8)). For each surplus company, allocation is `usable group loss × its remaining ordinary surplus / total remaining ordinary surpluses`. Preserve unused current/group-period losses for later use under the same ordering (§6(9)). A loss never becomes a transferable pre-group loss merely because a company was acquired.
4. Report the combined ordinary result on the parent's return using the special TAKS group schedule (§6(2)). A departing company retains its own unused pre-group and group-period losses (§7); the parent receives assessments/refunds under §8. Subsection 6(10) confines the stated debt-compromise loss reduction to the debtor company's own loss before the remaining group-period loss is used; obtain its debt/restructuring evidence before applying it.

wording: **Ordinary group control:** assume approved full-year grouping, no ownership-loss forfeiture or debt compromise, no separate capital-group permission, and C as parent. A has ordinary profit DKK 200,000, pre-group loss DKK 40,000 and own old group-period loss DKK 30,000, leaving DKK 130,000. C has DKK 70,000 ordinary profit. B has current ordinary loss DKK 100,000 and capital gain DKK 25,000 less old capital loss DKK 5,000. B first uses DKK 20,000 ordinary loss against its own net capital income; only DKK 80,000 remains for ordinary group allocation. A receives `80,000 × 130,000 / 200,000 = 52,000`; C receives DKK 28,000. Their final ordinary bases are DKK 78,000 and DKK 42,000: total DKK 120,000 and tax DKK 21,600 at the established 18% rate. B has no taxable capital remainder and no unused current ordinary loss in this fixture. [Regulation §6(3)–(9)][group]; [Capital Income Act §14][capital]; [Assessment Act §5(2)][rate]
